cards.lead: Waterborne spread of cholera shown in London
cards.name: Cholera spread through water, Broad Street and London
cards.summary: John Snow traced 1854 London cholera deaths to a contaminated street pump and then compared water companies, linking cholera to sewage-fouled water.
cards.description: In September 1854 John Snow suspected that the water of the Broad Street pump in Golden Square, London, was contaminated during a cholera outbreak. His 1855 book described how the Lambeth Company moved its works upstream to obtain water free from London sewage, a supply he set against that of the Southwark and Vauxhall Company.
cards.origin_note: The 1855 book and the 1854 inquiry are the earliest evidence opened here; Budd's and Pacini's parallel work was not checked, so priority is taken from the lead.

impact.note: Snow's method and water-supply argument shaped epidemiology and public health, as the lead scored it.

events.label: September 1854
events.statement: During the Broad Street outbreak in September 1854, Snow suspected contamination of the street pump's water.
events.quote: I suspected some contamination of the water of the much-frequented street pump in Broad Street
events.locator: Text of the 1855 second edition, account of the Broad Street outbreak

events.statement: Snow's 1855 book describes the Lambeth Company's 1852 move upstream, which gave it water free from London sewage, and sets that supply against the Southwark and Vauxhall Company's.
events.quote: The Lambeth Company removed their water works, in 1852, from opposite Hungerford Market to Thames Ditton; thus obtaining a supply of water quite free from the sewage of London.
events.locator: Text of the 1855 second edition, section on the Lambeth water supply

sources.title: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd edition)

open_questions: Snow's 1849 essay and the Southwark and Vauxhall comparison tables were not checked against an opened source beyond the 1855 text.

The popular story that the pump handle was removed is partly supported by the 1855 text (removed the day after Snow's remarks), but the account of the map as proof is disputed in secondary literature.
Coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge of the locations, and should be checked against a map source.

cards.lead: Mosquito transmission of yellow fever in Havana
cards.note: The 1881 proposal and the 1900 test are supported, but the sources opened do not say Finlay's idea was independent, so origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Mosquito transmission of yellow fever, Havana
cards.summary: Carlos Finlay proposed in 1881 that mosquitoes carried yellow fever; a US Army board tested the idea in Cuba in 1900.
cards.description: By 1881 Carlos Finlay had fixed on mosquitoes as the cause of yellow fever in Havana, but his theory was largely dismissed. In 1900 Walter Reed's US Army Yellow Fever Board decided to test Finlay's theory, with Jesse Lazear running the mosquito experiments.
cards.origin_note: The PBS account does not say whether Finlay knew of earlier work on mosquitoes and filariasis, so the independence claim is not settled by these sources.

impact.note: Naming the mosquito let Havana and Panama control yellow fever by attacking breeding sites, as the lead scored it.

events.statement: By 1881 Carlos Finlay had fixed on mosquitoes as the cause of yellow fever, but his theory was largely dismissed.
events.quote: By 1881 Finlay had fixed on mosquitoes as the cause, but his theory was largely dismissed.

events.statement: In 1900 Walter Reed's US Army Yellow Fever Board decided to test Finlay's mosquito theory in Cuba, with Jesse Lazear running the experiments.
events.quote: The board could find no other solution, so members decided to test Finlay's theory.

sources.title: Fever: Yellow Fever and the Scientific Method

open_questions: Whether Finlay knew of Manson's 1877 work on filariae in mosquitoes is not settled by the source opened.
The exact 1881 paper details and the 1900 proof reports were not opened; Gorgas's control campaigns from 1901 were not checked.
Coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge of Havana, and should be checked.

cards.lead: Mosquito transmission of malaria in India
cards.note: The 1897 Secunderabad work and the December 1897 publication are supported; the 1898 bird and human proofs, Grassi and Smith and Kilborne were not verified from opened sources.
cards.name: Mosquito transmission of malaria, Secunderabad
cards.summary: In 1897 Ronald Ross in Secunderabad showed that Anopheles mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite, a finding made possible by Patrick Manson's earlier advice.
cards.description: In 1897 Ronald Ross in Secunderabad, India, demonstrated that the Anopheles mosquito was crucial in the malaria transmission cycle. He published the discovery in the British Medical Journal in December 1897, having been prompted by Patrick Manson's suggestion that mosquitoes spread malaria.
cards.origin_note: Hektoen reports that Manson told Ross in 1894 that mosquitoes were connected with malaria, so the idea was transmitted and Ross's Indian work followed from it.

impact.note: Mosquito control of malaria with nets, drainage and insecticides followed the finding, as the lead scored it.

events.statement: In 1897 Ross, working in Secunderabad, showed that the Anopheles mosquito was crucial in the malaria transmission cycle.
events.quote: Sir Ronald Ross made pivotal contributions to this understanding in 1897 when he demonstrated that the Anopheles mosquito was crucial in the malaria transmission cycle.

events.label: 18 December 1897
events.statement: Ross published the discovery in the British Medical Journal on 18 December 1897.
events.quote: He published this discovery in the British Medical Journal issue from Dec 18, 1897

open_questions: Hektoen reports that in May 1895 Ross observed early stages of the parasite in a mosquito at Bombay; whether this counts as an earlier step is not settled here.
Ross's 1898 bird-malaria work, Grassi's 1898 human work and the Smith and Kilborne tick work of 1893 were not opened or checked.
Coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge of Secunderabad, and should be checked.

cards.lead: Proof that smoking causes lung cancer
cards.note: The 1950 Doll and Hill paper is a preliminary report, and the German study by Muller (1939) came first, so the lead's independence and proof framing do not hold. The 1954 study was not checked.
cards.name: Smoking linked to lung cancer, London
cards.summary: In 1950 Doll and Hill reported a preliminary study linking smoking to lung cancer, following earlier German evidence from 1939.
cards.description: In 1939 Muller's German study found that most male lung-cancer patients were heavy smokers. In September 1950 Richard Doll and A. Bradford Hill published a preliminary report on smoking and carcinoma of the lung in the British Medical Journal.
cards.origin_note: The 1950 report cites earlier German and American studies, so independence is not established by the source.

impact.note: Population evidence on smoking shaped later public health policy, as the lead scored it.

events.statement: Muller's 1939 German study found that 56 of 86 male lung-cancer patients were heavy smokers.
events.quote: in Germany, Muller (1939) found that only 3 out of 86 male patients with cancer of the lung were non-smokers, while 56 were heavy smokers

events.label: 30 September 1950
events.statement: Doll and Hill published a preliminary report on smoking and carcinoma of the lung in the British Medical Journal on 30 September 1950.
events.quote: SMOKING AND CARCINOMA OF THE LUNG PRELIMINARY REPORT BY RICHARD DOLL

sources.title: Smoking and Carcinoma of the Lung: Preliminary Report

open_questions: The 1954 British doctors study, the 1962 and 1964 reports and the American Wynder and Graham paper of 1950 were not opened.
Richard Doll's and Bradford Hill's birth and death years were not taken from an opened source.

cards.note: The 2010 Antiquity abstract dates coca chewing to 'by at least 8000 cal BP', about 6050 BCE, not c. 6000 BCE. The later cocaine and anaesthesia links were not checked.
cards.name: Coca chewing, Nanchoc Valley
cards.summary: Coca leaves found in house floors in Peru's Nanchoc Valley show that people chewed coca in South America by about 8,000 years ago.
cards.description: Excavated coca leaves from house floors in the Nanchoc Valley of northern Peru show that chewing coca in South America began by at least 8000 cal BP. The find was reported by Dillehay and colleagues in Antiquity in 2010.
cards.origin_note: The abstract presents these leaves as the earliest coca chewing it reports, and it makes no comparison with other Andean sites.

impact.note: Coca use sustained Andean work at altitude over millennia, as the lead scored it.

events.label: by about 6050 BCE
events.statement: Coca leaves found in house floors in the Nanchoc Valley show that coca chewing began by at least 8,000 years before present, about 6050 BCE.
events.quote: Chewing coca in South America began by at least 8000 cal BP: our authors found and identified coca leaves of that date in house floors in the Nanchoc Valley, Peru.

sources.title: Early Holocene coca chewing in northern Peru

open_questions: The full paper, with its dating and lime evidence, was not opened; the lime-and-coca interpretation comes from press reports and was not checked against it.
Cocaine's isolation (1860) and Koller's 1884 local anaesthesia were not checked.
Coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge of the valley, and should be checked.

cards.note: The source dates Sertürner's isolation between 1803 and 1805, with a first note in 1805, a comprehensive paper in 1817 and production from 1827, not the lead's 1804 to 1817.
cards.name: Isolation of morphine, Germany
cards.summary: Friedrich Sertürner isolated morphine, the first pure plant alkaloid, from opium in the early 1800s, and his 1817 paper established it.
cards.description: Friedrich Sertürner extracted the active ingredient of opium between 1803 and 1805 and named it morphium. He published a comprehensive paper on its isolation and chemistry in 1817, and production began in Darmstadt in 1827 by the pharmacy that became Merck.
cards.origin_note: The source credits Sertürner with first isolating the active ingredient of opium and naming it; no earlier isolation of morphine was found in the source.

impact.note: Pure alkaloid isolation made drug doses exact and started a family of plant-derived medicines, as the lead scored it.

events.label: 1803 to 1805
events.statement: Sertürner first isolated the active ingredient of opium between 1803 and 1805.
events.quote: was first isolated (extracted) from the opium poppy (Papaver Somniferum) between 1803 and 1805

events.statement: Sertürner's first recorded note on the sleep-inducing substance from opium appeared in a pharmacy journal in 1805.
events.quote: was in a letter to the editor of the Trommsdorff Journal de Pharmacie in 1805

events.statement: In 1817 Sertürner published a comprehensive paper on the isolation, crystallization and chemistry of the substance.
events.quote: Sertürner continued his research with the substance and, in 1817, published a comprehensive paper on its isolation, crystallization, crystal structure and chemical characterization.

events.statement: Morphine production began in Darmstadt in 1827, by the pharmacy that became Merck.
events.quote: in 1827, production of morphine began in Darmstadt, Germany, by the pharmacy that was to become the pharmaceutical company Merck

sources.title: Educational series 2, bulletin 9, vignette 4: The isolation of morphine
sources.publisher: International Network for the History of Neuropsychopharmacology

open_questions: Rival claims by Derosne and Seguin were not checked.
Paderborn and Einbeck, named in the lead, are not mentioned in the source opened; the place is given at country level.
Coordinates are approximate, from general knowledge of Germany, and should be checked.
